title: Aerial surveys of seabirds: the advent of digital methods

1. Aerial seabird surveys are often conducted so that changes in abundance may be monitored. For example, large‐scale offshore wind farms are proposed for UK waters, and surveys are currently being conducted to quantify numbers and distribution ahead of construction.
 2. Technological advances mean that strip transect surveys may now be conducted, using digital methods. We address survey design and data analysis issues for such digital surveys, contrasting them with visual aerial line transect surveys.
3. We also explore the relative performances of the methods for estimating the size of a large aggregation of common scoters in Carmarthen Bay, Wales. We found that abundance estimates from two digital methods were closely comparable, while estimates from visual aerial surveys were appreciably lower.
4. Synthesis and applications. Efficient survey methods to quantify abundance and distribution of seabirds are needed, to assess change arising from climate change, or developments such as the construction of large‐scale offshore wind farms. The traditional survey methods are visual surveys conducted along transects from ships or aircraft. Digital video and stills surveys can be conducted from aircraft flying sufficiently high to avoid disturbance, while still being able to detect and identify seabirds. Given the rapid technological developments, we expect digital surveys largely to replace visual surveys for seabirds in offshore regions.

## Aerial of seabirds: the advent of surveys digital methods

## Stephen T. Buckland[1] *, M. Louise Burt[1] , Eric A. Rexstad[1] , Matt Mellor[2] , Adrian E. Williams[3] and Rebecca Woodward[4]

> 1University of St Andrews, CREEM, The Observatory, Buchanan Gardens, St Andrews, Fife, KY16 9LZ, UK; 2Hidef Aerial Surveying, Phoenix Court, Earl Street, Cleator Moor, Cumbria, CA25 5AU, UK;[3] APEM Ltd., Remote Sensing Division, A17 Riverview, Embankment Business Park, Stockport, SK4 3GN, UK; and[4] WWT Consulting, Slimbridge, Gloucestershire, UK

## Summary

1. Aerial seabird surveys are often conducted so that changes in abundance may be monitored. For example, large-scale offshore wind farms are proposed for UK waters, and surveys are currently being conducted to quantify numbers and distribution ahead of construction.

2. Technological advances mean that strip transect surveys may now be conducted, using digital methods. We address survey design and data analysis issues for such digital surveys, contrasting them with visual aerial line transect surveys.

3. We also explore the relative performances of the methods for estimating the size of a large aggregation of common scoters in Carmarthen Bay, Wales. We found that abundance estimates from two digital methods were closely comparable, while estimates from visual aerial surveys were appreciably lower.

4. Synthesis and applications. Efficient survey methods to quantify abundance and distribution of seabirds are needed, to assess change arising from climate change, or developments such as the construction of large-scale offshore wind farms. The traditional survey methods are visual surveys conducted along transects from ships or aircraft. Digital video and stills surveys can be conducted from aircraft flying sufficiently high to avoid disturbance, while still being able to detect and identify seabirds. Given the rapid technological developments, we expect digital surveys largely to replace visual surveys for seabirds in offshore regions.

Key-words: digital surveys, impact assessment surveys, line transect sampling, plot sampling, stills photography, strip transect sampling, video, visual surveys

## Introduction

Aerial surveys of seabirds are often a cost-effective way to quantify abundance, and to assess changes in abundance and distribution, perhaps as a result of some impact to the environment. Because of technological advances, digital survey methods have become competitive with visual methods. The impetus for these technological developments was the need to assess the impact on seabird populations of large-scale offshore wind farm developments in UK waters. By July 2010, offshore wind power accounted for around 1200 MW of electricity generated, making the UK the country with the largest portfolio of offshore wind projects (Toke 2011). UK capacity is projected to increase more than tenfold, to reach at least 15% of UK electricity production by 2020 (Toke 2011). These

*Correspondence author. E-mail: steve@st-andrews.ac.uk

developments may have significant effects on seabird populations; turbine blades may cause mortality; habitat alteration may change food availability; noise and disturbance may lead to avoidance or behavioural changes. Several studies have considered impacts on seabirds (Garthe & Hu ̈ ppop 2004; Drewitt & Langston 2006; Fox et al. 2006; Stewart, Pullin & Coles 2007; Langston 2010; Masden et al. 2010).

Digital surveys are conducted using plot sampling methods. In plot sampling, a representative sample of plots or quadrats is distributed through the survey region, and the number of individuals in each plot counted. We assume that all individuals in a plot will be detected. Representativeness of the plots is ensured by adopting a randomized scheme. When digital stills surveys are conducted, the plot is naturally defined to be a single digital still, and the method is truly a snapshot method, avoiding bias arising from the movement of birds on and off the plot that can occur in a visual survey. For digital video

surveys, or digital stills surveys when successive photographs taken along the trackline are pasted together, we have a special case of plot sampling, termed strip transect sampling, in which the plots are long, narrow strips.

Aerial visual surveys are generally conducted using either strip transect sampling (Briggs, Tyler & Lewis 1985; Certain & Bretagnolle 2008) or line transect sampling (Buckland et al. 2001), which is an extension of strip transect sampling in which not all individuals in the strip need be detected.

We describe the digital stills and digital video survey methods in use and consider their pros and cons relative to visual surveys. We then compare the performance of both digital methods with each other and with visual aerial line transect methods for estimating the abundance of a large aggregation of common scoters Melanitta nigra in Carmarthen Bay on the Welsh coast. We use both design-based and model-based methods to analyse the data. The model-based analyses also allow us to compare how effective the respective methods are for quantifying the spatial distribution of scoters within the bay.

## Materials and methods

## SURVEY METHODS

We consider three types of survey: aerial visual surveys, conducted using line transect sampling; aerial digital video surveys, conducted using strip transect sampling; and aerial digital stills surveys, conducted using either strips or a grid (a systematic sample of plots).

## Aerial visual surveys

Buckland et al. (2001: 280–287) give a detailed discussion of aerial sightings surveys. Typically, parallel transects are spaced systematically (i.e. the spacing between successive transects is constant), with the distance between transects determined by the precision desired on abundance or density estimates, although line separation should be sufficient that birds flushed while traversing one survey strip are unlikely to move as far as the next strip. A pilot survey may be used to estimate the total effort required and hence the line spacing (Buckland et al. 2001: 240–244). Often, a zigzag transect layout (Strindberg & Buckland 2004) is used so that time is not wasted travelling between transects.

Given the speed at which aircraft move, it is more practical to record the perpendicular distance from the trackline directly than to measure sighting distance and angle. However, for surveys in which large aggregations may be encountered, it is not feasible to record distances to each individual bird detected; instead, birds are counted in each of a small number of distance intervals. These intervals are typically indicated by aligned markers on the windows and wing struts of the aircraft.

## Aerial digital video surveys

We do not give technical specifications of digital methods here as the rapid advances would lead to new specifications that supersede these within months. More information (now rather dated) is provided in Thaxter & Burton (2009).

Design issues for digital video surveys are largely as for visual aerial surveys. However, as the strip searched is narrower given the current

state of technology, the design should comprise more lines, more closely spaced than for visual surveys, to ensure comparable precision (Thaxter & Burton 2009).

In contrast with visual surveys, the camera covers a narrow strip more-or-less vertically below the aircraft, which flies at higher altitude. Provided the camera has been designed so that resolution is approximately constant across the field of view, detectability does not fall away with distance from the trackline. Thus, we assume that all birds in the covered strip are counted (strip transect sampling) or, in the case of intermittently available (e.g. diving) birds, that probability of detection is not a function of distance from the trackline.

## Aerial digital stills surveys

When stills surveys are conducted in the same way as video surveys, the strip comprises a series of still images, patched together. Alternatively, there may be gaps along the transect between successive stills. If this gap is made the same as the gap between successive transects, then a systematic sample (i.e. a grid) of squares results, and we can exploit this grid sampling design by assuming that the individual squares are independent, rather than whole strips as in strip transect sampling. This method gives many more sampling units and hence greater replication for estimating the variability in the number of birds seen per unit area. Whether the strategy is more effective than surveying complete strips depends largely on the spatial distribution of birds. Typically, we can expect higher precision for a fixed flight length if the images cover whole strips, but poorer estimates of that precision.

## COMPARING METHODS: SCOTERS IN CARMARTHEN BAY

In March 2009, aerial surveys of common scoters were conducted using the three aerial survey methods described here (visual, digital stills and digital video) on four days in the Carmarthen Bay Special Protection Area in Wales (5140¢N, 430¢W). Complete details of the surveys can be found in Burt, Rexstad & Buckland (2010). We present design- and model-based estimates of abundance combining the four survey replicates, treating them as a single survey that characterizes the average number of birds within the study area over the period covered by the replicate surveys. Because the true number of common scoters in Carmarthen Bay during this period is unknown, we cannot assess relative bias of the survey methods, but the comparison does offer insights into the performance of the three data collection methods and two analytical procedures.

## Digital surveys

For both digital surveys, strip transect sampling was carried out. For digital stills, a systematic grid of parallel transects was defined with 2 km separation between successive transects. The plane had a downward-pointing camera, which recorded images 330 m in width from an altitude of 457 m. For digital video, the design comprised a systematic grid of parallel transects with 1 km separation (and consequently around twice the number of transects). The plane had four forward-looking cameras (30–45 from vertical) each recording images 50 m in width at an altitude of 609 m; these four strips were separated by gaps in cover, to spread the spatial cover of the survey – the total width of video footprint was 200 m, but spread over a wider strip. More lines were flown, and so more segments were available for analysis, for the digital video surveys than for the digital stills surveys, so we expect it to yield higher precision.

## 962 S. T. Buckland et al.

The video data were manually annotated by a team of trained reviewers. Double review was carried out by different reviewers on 20% of the data, selected at random. Reviewers were unaware of when they were performing double reviews, although they were aware that some of the data were being checked. Where a double review was carried out, the detections for each transect were split into those found by both reviewers and those found by a single reviewer. For all transects, over 90% of detections were made by both reviewers. Detected birds were then handed on to expert reviewers for classification by species. The same process of double-blind review was applied to the species identification; again the agreement was found to be over 90% in all cases.

Digital stills were packaged into batches of 50 photographs and assigned to a reviewer. Photographs were manually assessed on highdefinition LCD screens. As the high-definition digital still images were large (2 · 1Æ3 m), the number of individual screen scans per photograph was kept identical across operators. All birds in an image were counted and their coordinates tagged in a GIS layer. Each bird was identified and assigned to one of the JNCC bird species ⁄ grouping classifications. A cropped shot of each bird was saved for subsequent validation. Images that contained no birds were marked as ‘blanks’. A quality assurance process was undertaken both to check that the correct number of birds had been counted and to confirm the identification of those birds. From each batch, 20% of the ‘blank’ images and 20% of the images containing birds were rechecked by a second reviewer. To avoid bias, the second reviewer did not know whether they were looking at a previously identified ‘blank’ image or an image containing birds, and they were unaware whether they were undertaking a first or second pass of an image. Within a batch, at least 90% agreement between reviewers was required for both ‘blanks’ and bird ‘counts’. This condition was always met; had it not been, that batch would have been reprocessed. All of the individually saved cropped bird images previously assigned to one of the JNCC bird species ⁄ groups were validated internally by a second reviewer. In cases of disagreement, a final assessment was provided by a third reviewer. Of the bird images, 20% were then audited externally by the British Trust for Ornithology. At least 90% agreement in bird identification was required and indeed achieved in all cases.

## Visual surveys

The visual surveys were conducted using line transect sampling methods (Buckland et al. 2001). Line transect sampling is an extension of strip transect sampling, in which not all individuals in the strip need be detected. In the basic method, it is assumed that all individuals on the trackline are detected, but the probability of detection is assumed to fall off smoothly from unity as a function of distance from the trackline; this function is termed the detection function.

As for the digital stills surveys, a systematic grid of transects was placed over the study region with 2 km separation between successive lines. The plane flew at 200 km h[)][1] at an altitude of 76 m, and observers were unable to see immediately below the plane. Detected birds were recorded in four perpendicular distance bands: 44–163 m; 163– 282 m; 282–426 m; and 426–1000 m. Detection functions were fitted to data from the first three bands; the few sightings made in the most distant band were truncated.

## Design-based analyses

Design-based inference assumes that the sampled plots constitute a random sample that is representative of the entire study area. Mean density for the sampling units visited is estimated and then applied to

the entire study area. Thus, we extend inference from the plots to the whole study area or stratum, relying on the survey design to ensure that the plots are representative.

For the digital surveys of scoter, the plots were long, narrow strips. We assume that all birds located in each strip were counted, so that the number counted divided by total strip area gives an estimate of density for the study region. The counts were analysed using strip transect methods by specifying a uniform detection function in software Distance (Thomas et al. 2010).

The visual survey data were analysed using the conventional distance sampling engine of Distance (Thomas et al. 2010). The line was assumed to be offset by 44 m, to allow for lack of visibility below the aircraft. Thus, birds at 44 m were assumed to be certain to be detected, and the fall-off in probability of detection out to the truncation distance of 426 m (corresponding to a strip half-width of 382 m) was modelled.

## Model-based analyses

Model-based inference extrapolates from the covered region to the entire study area based upon a model. The assumed model is fitted using data on the density of birds in portions of the covered region and predictive covariates such as water depth or sea surface temperature (Hedley & Buckland 2004). Inference is less dependent than for design-based methods on the covered region being a random sample of the study area, but requires that the model extrapolates reliably to the whole study area. In practice, this is more likely to be the case if sampling units are selected according to a randomized design. Values of any predictive covariates should be available throughout the study area. These values are used together with the fitted model to estimate the density of birds throughout the study area. A grid of cells is defined over the study area, and density is estimated in each cell. Summing these allows us to estimate abundance in the area, or in any subarea of interest. In this way, we can assess not only whether abundance is affected by a development or perturbation but also whether the spatial distribution of birds is affected.

For the scoter surveys, transects were divided into segments of length 1 km, resulting in 697 segments for the digital stills and the visual surveys and 1181 segments for the digital video surveys. Analyses were conducted using the density surface modelling engine of Distance (Thomas et al. 2010). The same covariates were used to model the data from all three sets of surveys: latitude and longitude of each cell in the study area along with distance from the coastline.

## Discussion

## ASSESSING CHANGES IN DENSITY OR DISTRIBUTION

The simplest method to test for a change in abundance because of some impact such as the construction of a wind farm is to obtain design-based estimates of mean density and associated variance both pre-impact and post-impact, and then to use a z-test or approximate t-test as outlined by Buckland et al. (2001: 84–86), to assess whether there has been a significant change in density. This could be done for the impact area (e.g. the footprint of a wind farm) and for areas thought to be unaffected by the impact, which might be regarded as controls. If there is adequate replication and precision in the surveys in both space and time, then a BACI (before–after controlimpact) survey design might be considered (e.g. de Lucas, Janss & Ferrer 2005; Lapen ̃ a et al. 2010), with the analysis proceeding as described by Buckland et al. (2009). Model-based estimates can be used in the same way, but they also allow us to assess whether there has been redistribution of birds within the study area. For example, model-based methods incorporating spatial autocorrelation were used by Petersen et al. (2011) in an impact study of the Nysted wind farm on long-tailed ducks Clangula hyemalis off the coast of Denmark. The methods allowed locations where there had been significant changes in abundance between pre- and post-construction to be identified. The study found that all significant declines were within the footprint of the wind farm, with some increases elsewhere, providing evidence that birds had redistributed away from the wind farm, while no overall change in abundance was detected.

Model-based methods can also be used to analyse pre-construction data, to help identify locations where wind farm

impact might be minimized, for example, in areas with low densities of the more vulnerable species.

## WHICH METHOD WHEN?

Surveys of seabirds have traditionally been undertaken using aerial or shipboard visual surveys (Buckland et al. 2001). However, visual methods cannot be validated after the event to assess reliability of counts and species identity, and digital surveys are now taking preference in UK waters, given that improving technology ensures ever-increasing reliability and quality assurance.

For shipboard visual surveys, the width of the covered strip centred on the trackline is large, so that encounter rates are typically higher than for aerial surveys. For diving birds, the probability that a bird that is on the trackline is detected tends to be closer to the assumed value of one than for aerial surveys, because any point on the trackline is in view for much longer (Buckland et al. 2001:288). If it is appreciably below one, double-platform methods are well developed for shipboard surveys, to allow its estimation (Borchers et al. 2006; Buckland, Laake & Borchers 2010). On the negative side, shipboard surveys are costly (high operational costs, together with long travel times to and from the survey region), the speed of the platform is slow, special methods must be used for flying seabirds to avoid severe bias (Tasker et al. 1984; Spear, Nur & Ainley 1992; Buckland et al. 2001:202,288), responsive movement (often attraction to the vessel) prior to detection can generate substantial bias in estimates (Buckland et al. 2001:32,288), and ships may be unable to survey within the impact area if there is a perceived hazard to navigation, compromising random placement of transects post-construction. Distances at sea are difficult to estimate accurately. Typically, binoculars with reticles (Buckland et al. 2001: 255–259) or callipers (Heineman 1981) are used to estimate sighting (birdto-observer) distances from ships, and the sighting angle is also recorded (Buckland et al. 2001: 263–264), from which the perpendicular distance of the detected bird from the trackline is estimated (Buckland et al. 2001: 5).

Aerial visual surveys are quick and inexpensive relative to shipboard surveys (Buckland et al. 2001:280; Certain & Bretagnolle 2008). Although the aircraft fly at an altitude that causes disturbance, birds have less time to respond than for shipboard surveys, so that with the right aircraft and observer search pattern (so that birds are detected before they respond, or at least before they have time to move far or dive), biases

from responsive movement can largely be avoided (Buckland et al. 2001:280). When the surveys are to assess the impact of wind farm construction, aerial visual surveys often cannot be conducted within the footprint of the wind farm because of the risk of collision with turbine blades. If visual surveys can be conducted within the footprint, then transect placement is not random with respect to turbine location, which may bias results. For diving birds, probability of detection of birds on the trackline tends to be lower than for shipboard surveys, and methods to estimate this probability are not easily implemented. If double-observer methods are used, it may be necessary to have two aircraft flying in tandem (Hiby & Lovell 1998), given the difficulties in modelling the dependence between detections if both observers are on the same aircraft. In this case, separation of the aircraft needs to be given careful consideration, to take account of typical dive patterns of the species of interest. Another solution is to record birds at the surface, and separately (but synchronously in case the proportion varies in time and space), to estimate the proportion of time spent at the surface. In this case, care must be taken to define ‘at the surface’ (e.g. bird is on the surface, or breaking the surface, when abeam of the aircraft).

For digital video and stills surveys, images are available for independent verification. For a wide range of species, birds at the surface are virtually certain to be detected if they are within the covered strip. Aircraft can operate at a height to avoid disturbance and turbine blades. The problem of estimating the probability of detecting a bird on the trackline for diving species is simpler, as availability is well defined: it is whether the bird is available to be detected at the instant the image is taken (for stills), or at the instant it intersects an arbitrary line perpendicular to the transect (video). However, an estimate of the proportion of time birds are available is needed if absolute abundance or density is to be estimated, and this estimate should ideally come from a synchronous survey of a representative sample of birds, as the proportion may vary by space and time. Such a survey may present logistical difficulties, and be costly. Alternatively, double-observer methods might be applied to images of the same area of sea taken at slightly

Digital methods have potential for automation for locating and identifying birds in the images. Video and stills surveys need greater lengths of transect for comparable precision with aerial visual surveys, if the covered strips are narrower. The difference can be reduced by use of multiple cameras on a single aircraft or cameras with larger footprints. Given rapid advances in technology, we anticipate that digital surveys may soon be using strips whose widths are comparable with the effective width of strips (taking account of imperfect detectability in the strip) for visual aerial surveys and with fewer errors in misidentifying species.

For digital surveys, aircraft fly at much higher altitude than for visual surveys, and the strip covered is currently relatively narrow. Hence, there is unlikely to be any fall-off in detectability across the strip. Further, because locations of birds are known precisely, it is straightforward to test whether detected birds can be assumed to be uniformly distributed across the

strip, thus justifying a strip transect sampling analysis. By contrast, if strip transect sampling is used for visual surveys, a narrow strip must be selected. Briggs, Tyler & Lewis (1985) used strips of width 50 m, stating that they found downward bias for wider strips. This negates the major advantage of visual surveys, that a wide strip can be covered, increasing both sample size and percentage of the survey region that is sampled. The second point is especially important for species with aggregated distributions, such as scoters. Another disadvantage of using strip transect sampling for visual surveys is that the appropriate width of the strip varies by species, so that for multi-species surveys, the choice must be a compromise, and not ideal for most species. Certain & Bretagnolle (2008) argued for a strip width of 150 m, much wider than the 50 m recommended by Briggs, Tyler & Lewis (1985).

The Carmarthen Bay surveys of common scoter provide no evidence to favour either digital survey method. The precision of each method is largely driven by the proportion of the survey region that is surveyed, and how the sampling units are spread through the region. In the Carmarthen Bay study, the total area of the surveyed strips was similar, but the digital video surveys used more, narrower strips than did the digital stills surveys, which had a larger single footprint. The digital video surveys flew almost twice as many transects, so that survey effort was spread more evenly through the study area, and because scoter distributions are so aggregated, more precise estimates were obtained. However, both methods offer flexibility in how much of the study area is counted and in how that effort is distributed through the area; with equal air time, we see no reason to favour one approach over the other.

In marked contrast to the consistency in estimates from the digital surveys, the visual surveys gave much lower abundance estimates. Common scoters are one of the most problematic species for visual surveys. Scoter flocks tend to be highly aggregated, so that observers can be ‘swamped’, and scoters are sensitive to disturbance (Kaiser 2004), and so more prone than most other species to being flushed by the plane into the outer distance bands; hence, they are a challenging species for observers to count accurately (WWT Consulting 2009).

## COMPARING ESTIMATES OBTAINED FROM DIFFERENT SURVEY METHODS

Digital video and stills surveys are replacing visual aerial surveys for monitoring wind farm impacts on seabirds in UK waters (Thaxter & Burton 2009). Before winter 2009, preconstruction aerial surveys were carried out as visual surveys (Thaxter & Burton 2009). If post-construction surveys are conducted using video or stills surveys, this raises the question of whether estimates are comparable. There are two strategies that might be adopted. The first is to seek unbiased estimation from both approaches, so that estimates are directly comparable. The second strategy is to calibrate the methods, so that both methods are applied at the same time and place, and a correction (termed a calibration factor) obtained as the ratio of abundance or density estimates for the two approaches. Synchronous surveys generate strongly correlated estimates of

abundance from each method, which improves the precision of the estimated calibration factor. We recommend that the design and frequency of synchronous surveys should acknowledge that the calibration factor is unlikely to be constant across species, locations or seasons.

For future surveys, the more cost-effective solution may be to ensure that post-construction surveys are undertaken using the same methodology as pre-construction surveys.

The dangers of confounding impact and changes in technology are less if we concentrate on identifying changes in spatial distribution before and after construction, rather than on changes in abundance. Typically, however, regulators require surveys to quantify abundance as well as spatial distribution.

## ASSESSING IMPACT

When the methods of this paper are used for identifying changes in abundance and distribution of seabirds in response to the construction of, for example, an offshore wind farm, if we are to have confidence that identified changes are caused by the wind farm, a number of issues must be addressed. The survey design should incorporate repeat surveys in several years leading up to wind farm construction, and again for several years post-construction, as numbers within the region of the wind farm may vary appreciably for reasons unassociated with the wind farm. During the surveys, efforts should be made to record relevant environmental variables that might influence distribution and abundance (Garthe et al. 2009), so that these can be incorporated in density surface models, allowing change caused by environmental conditions to be appropriately attributed. If any changes are considered to be caused by the wind farm, it is important to distinguish between a re-distribution of the population perhaps in response to disturbance (especially during the construction phase), and a reduction in abundance, perhaps because of a raised mortality rate resulting from collisions with turbine blades and ⁄ or a reduction in the available food resources.

If interest is only in whether the distribution of birds within the region has changed, rather than whether abundance has changed, then this may be assessed without the need for calibration when different survey methods are used pre- and post-construction, for example, by scaling both pre- and post-construction density surfaces to have the same average value. The resulting surfaces would then indicate where aggregations occur, and positive and negative differences between the surfaces would identify changes of location of aggregations. However, they would not allow assessment of changes in abundance, and so this approach may not meet the current needs of regulators.

We consider that model-based methods should be preferred for impact assessment studies, as they are much more effective at identifying shifts of distribution of seabirds; for design-based methods, such shifts can only be identified by comparing stratum-specific abundance estimates, and the power of such comparisons depends strongly on where stratum boundaries are located, relative to the location of aggregations of birds pre- and post-construction.

## Conclusion

The advent of digital methods for surveying animal populations presents new challenges and opportunities for wildlife population assessment. When changes in surveying technology are coincident with long-term assessment of impacts, care needs to be paid to the method of assessing impacts. Modern model-based analysis methods allow identification of more subtle types of impact on seabirds by estimating spatial redistribution of birds as a result of wind farm operation.
